# Arithmetic and signed concave buffers: original-volume advantage and exact obstructions

This note evaluates two alternatives to the logarithmically normalized
positive parameter. Arithmetic normalization does formally produce the
desired **original uniform volume** target at a strictly positive
parameter minimum. Its positivity boundary is a real obstruction even
for the full class of continuous concave functions on an actual body.
Allowing arbitrary signed additive buffers avoids that boundary but
destroys the small-buffer approximation. Both assertions below have
exact actual-body certificates.

The affine-base boundary example in
`candidate 3101206ec4580190`,
§8, is a dependency and is not new. Section 3 below strengthens it from
affine parameters to **all full-space concave parameters**. No example
is below the OC target, and no joint body-minimum conclusion is asserted.

## 1. The genuine arithmetic-normalization benefit

Fix an actual finite positive-fiber mixed body, its measure \(\mu\),
and (M=\mu(S)). Put (N=d+1) and consider

\[
 L>0\text{ concave},\qquad \frac1M\int L\,d\mu=1,
 \qquad f_L=(LE/M)^{1/N}.                         \tag{1}
\]

The joint concavity proof is unchanged: write (E^{1/d}) and use the
weighted geometric mean with (L). Full-space dependence changes the
continuous alignment by \(\nabla_X L/(NL)\), exactly as for the
logarithmic parameter; that term must not be omitted.

For a fixed-body perturbation (L+t h\), arithmetic renormalization gives

\[
 \dot L=h-L\langle h\rangle,\qquad
 \dot{\log f_i}=\frac1N\left(\frac{h(Y_i)}{L_i}
                                      -\langle h\rangle\right),
 \quad \langle h\rangle=\frac1M\int h\,d\mu.       \tag{2}
\]

Suppose the actual selected response/cleanup argument at a strictly
positive minimum supplies normalized nonnegative contact weights
\(\sigma_i\), \(\sum\sigma_i=1\), with

\[
 \sum_i\frac{\sigma_i}{L_i}h(Y_i)\ge\langle h\rangle
                  \quad\text{for every concave }h. \tag{3}
\]

This paragraph is a conditional calculation of the resulting dual,
not a new proof of the nonregular response theorem. Because (L) has a
positive floor, every bounded signed affine (h\) is feasible in both
signs. Constants and affine coordinates in (3) therefore give equal
mass and barycenter. Thus

\[
 \sum_i\frac{\sigma_i}{L_i}\delta_{Y_i}
                  \ \le_{cx}\ \frac{\mu}{M}.       \tag{4}
\]

Unlike the logarithmic normalization, the target here is the original
uniform volume and has no (1/L\) density. This is a real benefit.

Nonnegative arithmetic normalization also gives uniform sampled bounds:

\[
 \sup_{K_z}L\le\frac{(d+1)M}{V_z},\qquad
             0\le f_L\le(d+1)^{1/N}.              \tag{5}
\]

For the first bound, if a nonnegative concave function has maximum (A\)
at a point of a (d\)-body, its superlevel of height (tA\) contains a
homothetic copy of the whole body of scale (1-t\); layer cake gives
integral at least (AV_z/(d+1)\). Approximation handles an unattained
supremum. Then use (E_z\le V_z\). Thus fixed-body buffered values stay
within (O(\epsilon)\) of ordinary values uniformly in this entire
nonnegative parameter class. The trouble is not escape to large sampled
values: it is attainment at zero.

## 2. Actual three-interval geometry and all-slope formula

At bases (P=\{-1,0,1\}\), take the centered intervals of lengths

\[
 (V_-,V_0,V_+)=(1/8,1,1),\qquad M=17/8.          \tag{6}
\]

Their half-length roof is concave, so their canonical hull is an actual
convex body with exactly these integer fibers. Its full mixed centroid is

\[
 \bar Y=(7/17,0).
\]

All fibers are strictly lighter than (M/2=17/16\). All proper closed
minor quotas are strict: singletons have one parity and mass (<M/2\);
the two consecutive pairs have two parities and mass (<M\). The
nonconsecutive endpoint pair is not closed.

Write (F_v(t)=\min(v,\max(v/2-t,0))\). For (a\le b\), direct interval
clipping gives the exact tilted endpoint infimum

\[
 \inf_s[F_a(h+s)+F_b(h-s)]
       =\min\{a,((a+b)/2-2h)_+\}.                \tag{7}
\]

To check the lower bound, if neither summand is saturated, their sum is
\((a+b)/2-2h\). Saturating the smaller interval at full mass gives at
least (a\), and saturating it at zero leaves the other summand at least
the displayed minimum; the two remaining statuses give the same bounds.
The infimum is attained either by a sufficiently steep finite tilt
(small interval full, large empty), or by placing the larger threshold
at its upper endpoint. This also covers full/empty transitions.

Consequently the unique ordinary deepest point is (Y=(0,0)\), with
raw value (Q=5/8\): its own interval contributes (1/2\), and (7)
contributes (1/8\). At a nonzero middle mark one of the two steep
orientations gives at most (5/8-|y|\). The endpoint maxima are exactly
(1/16,1/2\), by finite outward isolation. Pure-base depths are
(1/8,9/8,1\), respectively.

## 3. Unique boundary optimum over ALL full-space concave parameters

Let (L\ge0\) be continuous and concave on the canonical body of (6),
with original-volume arithmetic mean one. At the interior point (Y\),
choose a finite supporting affine majorant

\[
 A(z,x)=\ell+a z+b x,\qquad \ell=L(Y).
\]

Since (A\ge L\ge0\) at both endpoints of the small fiber,

\[
 a\le\ell-|b|/16\le\ell.
\]

Integrating the majorant and using the actual mixed centroid yields

\[
 1\le\ell+(7/17)a\le(24/17)\ell,
 \qquad L(Y)\ge17/24.                            \tag{8}
\]

Equality forces (a=\ell\), (b=0\), and (L=A\) almost everywhere on
every fiber. Continuity gives equality on the sampled fibers; concavity
and the same majorant give equality on their canonical hull. Thus the
unique equality parameter is

\[
 L_*(z,x)=\frac{17}{24}(1+z).                    \tag{9}
\]

This is nonnegative but zero on the **entire actual small endpoint
fiber**. For a class allowing irrelevant downward boundary values,
uniqueness means its canonical continuous representative; (8) and the
objective do not depend on such null-set values.

For the invariant energy buffer in (1),

\[
 \Sigma=1025/13056,\qquad E_0(y)=1-4y^2.
\]

For (0<\epsilon\le10^{-4}\), the complete buffered maximum at (9) is

\[
 Q_*(\epsilon)=\frac58+\epsilon\sqrt{\Sigma/3},  \tag{10}
\]

attained uniquely at (Y\). Indeed the own shift at (Y\) is
\(\delta_* =\epsilon\sqrt{\Sigma/3}\). The ordinary all-normal lower
bound gains exactly this proper own-interval length, while endpoint
contributions are nondecreasing; the steep caps attain equality. At
other middle marks the same two caps give
\(5/8-|y|+\epsilon\sqrt{\Sigma L_*(0)E_0(y)/M}\), uniquely maximized
at zero. Endpoint isolation and (5) give maximum at most
\(1/2+\epsilon\sqrt{2\Sigma}<5/8\).

For an arbitrary admissible (L\), (8) and monotonicity in the scalar
buffer imply its value at (Y\) is at least (10). If (L(Y)>17/24\),
the inequality is strict: starting at \(\delta_*\), every nonvertical
cap gains a common positive amount on its proper own interval for a
sufficiently small buffer increase, and both pure-base choices have a
strict gap. Larger increases preserve that strict gain by monotonicity.
Thus (9) is the unique global fixed-body parameter optimum in the full
nonnegative concave class. The strictly positive class has the same
infimum and **no minimizer**.

The same proof works for the simpler direct buffer (f=L\), normalized
by \(\langle L\rangle=1\), with physical norm \(|u|\). Its exact optimum
is (5/8+(17/24)\epsilon\), again uniquely at (9). For this direct class,
(5)'s first bound keeps the endpoint shifts (O(\epsilon)\); (9) gives
the exact all-source upper bound. This version need not vanish at own
fiber boundaries and is stated separately from the energy construction.

## 4. Exact boundary multiplier: why the original-volume row is absent

At (9) the only deepest source is (Y=(0,0)\), but the original mixed
centroid is ((7/17,0)\). No martingale from a probability supported at
that source to \(\mu/M\) exists.

There is instead an exact boundary-slack row. Put (Z=(-1,0)\), so
\(L_*(Z)=0\). Then

\[
 \frac{24}{17}\delta_Y
 \ \le_{cx}\ \frac\mu M+\frac7{17}\delta_Z.       \tag{11}
\]

The two sides have mass (24/17\), and the right side has barycenter
zero. Jensen, or the single row with this normalized target law, proves
(11) for every convex function. Equivalently every concave feasible
direction (h\), nonnegative on the zero set, satisfies

\[
 \frac{24}{17}h(Y)
 \ge\langle h\rangle+\frac7{17}h(Z)
 \ge\langle h\rangle.                            \tag{12}
\]

The extra target mass is supported where the parameter vanishes and is
complementary to (L_*\). It cannot be deleted while retaining the
original first moment. This obstruction has actual compatibility,
strict quotas, a unique deepest source, proper own critical traces,
and global full-concave parameter optimality. It has no joint body
minimality claim.

Arithmetic normalization also lacks the logarithmic zero-cut gain.
If a body cut removes mass (a\) and (r=\int_RL\,d\mu\), then rescaling
the retained parameter back to arithmetic mean one multiplies it by

\[
 \frac{M-a}{M-r}=1-\frac{a-r}{M-r}.              \tag{13}
\]

On a zero-level cut (L<t\), (r\le ta\). The gain is only (O(a)\),
not (a|\log t|\). Hence the proved logarithmic domination over other
first-order body responses does not carry over. A separate joint-shape
argument might still rule out zero at a genuinely bad minimum; (11)
shows why parameter stationarity alone cannot do it.

## 5. Unrestricted signed additive normalization destroys regularization

Keep the same actual body, but allow a directly signed concave buffer
of original arithmetic mean one. For (0<\epsilon\le10^{-4}\) choose

\[
 f_\epsilon(z,x)=1+\frac{z-7/17}{8\epsilon}.       \tag{14}
\]

This is affine, so it belongs to every full-space signed concave class
containing affine functions. Its physical threshold shifts are

\[
 (\delta_-,\delta_0,\delta_+)
 =\left(\epsilon-\frac3{17},\quad
         \epsilon-\frac7{136},\quad
         \epsilon+\frac5{68}\right).            \tag{15}
\]

At an endpoint source, finite outward isolation and the own interval
give maximum \(\min(V_z,(V_z/2+\delta_z)_+)\). Hence the left maximum
is zero, and the right maximum is (39/68+\epsilon\).

At the middle center, (7) applies with
\(h=-\delta_0=7/136-\epsilon<7/32=(1-1/8)/4\), so the endpoint
infimum is exactly (1/8\). The middle value is also

\[
 \frac12+\delta_0+\frac18=\frac{39}{68}+\epsilon.
\]

For every other middle mark, the two steep caps give the upper bound
\(1/8+(1/2-|y|+\delta_0)_+\), no greater than this center value.
Both continuous orientations and all tilts have been included in (7);
the pure-base gaps persist. Therefore the **global exact** value is

\[
 Q_\epsilon=\frac{39}{68}+\epsilon,
 \qquad Q_0^{\rm ordinary}=\frac58,
 \qquad \frac58-\frac{39}{68}=\frac7{136}.        \tag{16}
\]

Thus this normalized signed class has a fixed-body infimum at most a
quantity separated below ordinary depth by a positive constant as
\(\epsilon\downarrow0\). The multiplier grows as (1/\epsilon\), and
the physical shift does not vanish. With the fixed invariant interval
norm, absorb its positive constant \(\sqrt\Sigma\) into the coefficient
in (14); the same conclusion follows.

This obstruction also applies if one adds unrestricted signed affine
mean-zero functions to any fixed bounded nonnegative concave buffer
\(f_0\). Take (h_\epsilon=(z-7/17)/(8\epsilon)\). The remaining
\(\epsilon f_0\) shifts are uniformly (O(\epsilon)\), and the finite
interval strip bound makes the limit in (16) unchanged. Such a class
therefore cannot be used as an automatically vanishing regularization.

## 6. Precise comparison of the alternatives

* Positive arithmetic normalization would yield the original-volume
  martingale (4), and its nonnegative closure has a uniformly small
  buffer. The exact full-concave optimum can lie at zero, where the
  actual dual is (11) with additional boundary mass.
* Unrestricted signed additive normalization removes the positivity
  boundary but admits the nonvanishing shifts (15), so it can change
  the limiting ordinary minimization problem.
* A fixed compact bound or a penalty could suppress (14), but its
  active constraint or derivative enters the parameter dual. No claim
  that the original-volume martingale then survives is made here.

These are scoped stopping tests for the two proposed modifications,
not a claim that every new normalization or joint-shape argument fails.
